title: Property Tax Calculator by State: Estimate Your Annual Bill

answerSnippet: Property tax equals your home's value times your area's effective property tax rate. Rates vary enormously by state: New Jersey averages about 2.38% and Illinois 2.32%, while Hawaii is just 0.28% and Alabama 0.43%. On a $400,000 home that is roughly $9,520 a year in New Jersey versus $1,120 in Hawaii. This calculator uses average effective rates by state; your actual county or city rate can differ, so you can also enter a custom rate.
intro:
Property tax is one of the largest ongoing costs of owning a home, and it varies more by location than almost any other homeowner expense. This calculator estimates your **annual property tax** — and the **monthly amount** that shows up in your mortgage escrow — based on your home's value and your **state's average effective tax rate**.

The math is simple: **home value × effective rate = annual tax**. What is not simple is the rate. It ranges from about **0.28% in Hawaii** to roughly **2.38% in New Jersey** — an **8x difference**. On the same $400,000 home, that is the gap between a ~$1,100 and a ~$9,500 yearly bill. Because taxes are set locally, your specific county, city, or school district rate can be higher or lower than the state average, so the tool lets you enter a **custom rate** for a precise estimate.

Use it to compare the true cost of buying in different states, budget for escrow, sanity-check an assessment, or estimate the carrying cost of a home before you make an offer. The average rates come from Tax Foundation and U.S. Census data on owner-occupied housing.

example.title: Example: $400,000 home in New Jersey
steps: The same home in Hawaii (0.28%) would owe just $1,120 a year.

explanation:
## How property tax is calculated

```
Annual property tax = Assessed/home value × effective tax rate
Monthly (escrow)    = Annual ÷ 12
Per $1,000 of value = effective rate × 10
```

The **effective rate** is property tax actually paid as a share of home value — it already blends the local mill rate and any assessment ratio, which makes it the fairest way to compare states.

## Highest and lowest property tax states

| State | Effective rate | Tax on a $400,000 home |
|---|---|---|
| New Jersey | 2.38% | $9,520 |
| Illinois | 2.32% | $9,280 |
| New Hampshire | 2.15% | $8,600 |
| Texas | 1.68% | $6,720 |
| National average | ~0.90% | ~$3,600 |
| California | 0.75% | $3,000 |
| Alabama | 0.43% | $1,720 |
| Hawaii | 0.28% | $1,120 |

## Why 'no income tax' states can still be pricey

States like **Texas** and **New Hampshire** have **no state income tax**, but they lean on **property tax** to fund schools and services — so their property tax rates are among the highest. A low income-tax bill can be offset by a high property-tax bill, which is why total tax burden matters more than any single tax.

## Worked example — comparing two offers

You are choosing between a $450,000 home in **Ohio (1.53%)** and one in **Colorado (0.55%)**:
- Ohio: $450,000 × 1.53% = **$6,885/year** (~$574/month).
- Colorado: $450,000 × 0.55% = **$2,475/year** (~$206/month).
- The Ohio home costs about **$368 more per month** in property tax alone — real money in your mortgage payment.

## Important caveats

The state figures here are **averages**. Your actual bill depends on your **county, city, and school district**, plus:
- **Assessment ratio** — some places tax a fraction of market value, not the full value.
- **Homestead exemptions** — many states reduce the taxable value for a primary residence, seniors, veterans, or disabled owners.
- **Assessment caps** — California's Prop 13, for example, limits how fast assessed value can rise, so long-time owners often pay far below the average.

For an exact number, check your local assessor's website or a recent tax bill, and enter that rate in the **custom** field.

## Disclaimer

Educational estimate using average effective rates from Tax Foundation and U.S. Census data. Actual property taxes are set locally and vary by county, exemptions, and assessment practices. Verify with your county assessor.

faq.a: Multiply your home's **assessed value** by the local **effective tax rate**. For example, a $400,000 home at a 1.5% rate owes **$6,000 a year**. The effective rate blends the local mill rate and assessment ratio, so it is the simplest way to estimate and compare bills.

faq.q: Which states have the highest property taxes?
faq.a: **New Jersey (~2.38%)**, **Illinois (~2.32%)**, **New Hampshire (~2.15%)**, and **Connecticut (~1.98%)** have the highest average effective rates. On a typical home these states can mean $8,000–$10,000+ in annual property tax.

faq.q: Which states have the lowest property taxes?
faq.a: **Hawaii (~0.28%)** is the lowest, followed by **Alabama (~0.43%)**, **Louisiana (~0.51%)**, and **Delaware/Colorado/Nevada (~0.55%)**. Hawaii's low rate is partly offset by very high home prices, so the dollar bill is not always as low as the rate suggests.

faq.q: Do states with no income tax have higher property tax?
faq.a: Often, yes. **Texas** and **New Hampshire** have no state income tax but rank among the **highest property-tax** states because local governments rely on property tax for schools and services. Always compare the **total** tax burden, not just one tax.

A **homestead exemption** lowers the taxable value of your **primary residence**, reducing your bill. Amounts and eligibility vary widely by state, and many offer extra relief for **seniors, veterans, and disabled homeowners**. Check your county assessor to see what you qualify for.

faq.q: Why is my bill different from this estimate?
faq.a: This uses **state averages**. Your actual rate is set by your **county, city, and school district**, and depends on your assessment ratio and any exemptions. Two homes of equal value in the same state can have different bills. Use the **custom rate** field with your local rate for accuracy.

faq.q: Is property tax included in my mortgage payment?
faq.a: Usually. Most lenders collect **1/12 of your annual property tax each month** into an **escrow account** and pay the bill for you. That is why your total monthly payment (PITI) is higher than principal and interest alone — this calculator shows that monthly escrow amount.

faq.q: How often do property taxes go up?
faq.a: Bills typically change **yearly** as assessments and local budgets change. Some states cap how fast assessed value can rise (California's Prop 13 limits it to 2% a year), while others reassess to market value regularly — which can cause bills to jump after home prices rise.
